meta.case_name: Green Machine hybrid car pricing in Australia

prompt.context: Green Machine is a domestic car manufacturer in Australia and wants to launch an electric-hybrid compact-sedan in Australia. They have hired your team to help them formulate a pricing strategy.
prompt.question: How should Green Machine price its new electric-hybrid car in Australia?

clarifying_info.q: Is Green Machine an established player or a new entrant?
clarifying_info.a: Green Machine is a domestic car manufacturer in Australia.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the Australian car market?
clarifying_info.a: About 700,000 cars per year, of which 80% are sedans.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any competitor hybrid vehicles currently in Australia?
clarifying_info.a: There are currently no hybrid vehicles in the mainstream in Australia. However, Toyota and Honda are planning to launch hybrids in Australia in about 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: What are comparable hybrid cars selling for in other markets?
clarifying_info.a: Hybrid cars were introduced about 7 years ago in the US. Toyota sells the Prius at about $35,000 and Honda sells the Civic Hybrid at about $31,000.

clarifying_info.q: What is the fuel efficiency of the hybrid vs. non-hybrid?
clarifying_info.a: Green Machine hybrids achieve 40 mpg in the city and 33 mpg on the highway. Non-hybrid sedans average 20 mpg in the city and 25 mpg on the highway.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of gasoline in Australia?
How many miles does an average Australian car owner drive per year?
How long does the average owner keep a car?
What is the maintenance cost difference for hybrids?
clarifying_info.a: Hybrid cars have a higher maintenance cost — about $125 per year more than conventional cars.

clarifying_info.q: What does a non-hybrid sedan sell for?
What is the cost to manufacture the hybrid?
clarifying_info.a: Manufacturing cost is about $20,000. Distribution expenses are an additional 10% and Sales & Marketing expenses are an additional 15% of manufacturing cost.
Apart from waiving taxes, the government is willing to give a $1,000 subsidy per hybrid car sold.

clarifying_info.q: Are there consumer survey data on willingness to pay?
clarifying_info.a: In a consumer survey, about 15,000 consumers said they will pay $35,000 for a hybrid within the next 3 years; 10,000 said they will pay $30,000; and 25,000 said they will pay $27,500.

framework: Value-based pricing: calculate the incremental value a hybrid delivers to a customer vs. a conventional sedan (fuel savings minus extra maintenance cost, over the car's life)
Cost-plus pricing: calculate total cost to manufacture and sell the hybrid, including distribution and S&M, then assess whether a margin is achievable
Competitive pricing: benchmark against comparable hybrids in other markets (Prius ~$35K, Civic Hybrid ~$31K) and against domestic non-hybrid sedans ($20K–$23K)
Supply-and-demand / willingness-to-pay pricing: use survey data to model revenue and profit at different price points and select the profit-maximizing price

Skimming strategy: given a 3-year window before competitors enter, evaluate pricing above the value-based ceiling to capture early adopters willing to pay a premium, then reduce prices as competition arrives

questions.prompt: Using value-based pricing, what is the maximum premium a customer should rationally be willing to pay for the hybrid over a conventional sedan?
questions.guidance: The candidate should calculate annual fuel cost for hybrid vs. non-hybrid, subtract incremental maintenance, multiply net annual saving by 5 years of ownership, then add this to the conventional sedan price to get a value-based ceiling.

math.setup: Compare annual fuel cost for hybrid and non-hybrid given 20,000 miles/yr (50% city, 50% highway), then net out $125/yr extra maintenance, multiply by 5 years.
steps: Hybrid gallons city: 10,000/40 = 250; Non-hybrid gallons city: 10,000/20 = 500
Hybrid gallons highway: 10,000/33 ≈ 303 (casebook rounds to 300); Non-hybrid gallons highway: 10,000/25 = 400
Net annual saving after extra maintenance: $1,225 - $125 = $1,100

questions.prompt: Using cost-plus pricing, what is the total cost per hybrid car to Green Machine, and does the value-based price range cover a margin?
questions.guidance: The candidate should add up manufacturing, distribution, and S&M costs, then subtract the government subsidy. Taxes are waived. Compare total cost against the value-based price range to confirm viability.

math.setup: Start with $20,000 manufacturing cost, add 10% distribution and 15% S&M, subtract $1,000 government subsidy.
math.answer: Total cost per car = $24,000; the value-based range of $25,500–$28,500 is above cost, so the strategy is viable.

questions.prompt: Given the consumer survey data and a 3-year window before competition enters, which price maximizes total profit? Should Green Machine consider a price-skimming strategy?
questions.guidance: The candidate should model revenue and profit at each price point. Key insight: at $35,000 only the 15,000 highest-WTP consumers buy; at $30,000 those 15,000 plus the next 10,000 = 25,000 (but casebook uses cumulative: 20,000 at $30K and 55,000 at $27,500 — note the casebook appears to use cumulative demand). The candidate should identify $35,000 as profit-maximizing, then recommend skimming: launch at $35,000 to capture early adopters and premium segment for 3 years, then slash prices to attract the broader market when Toyota/Honda enter.

math.setup: For each price point, compute revenue = price × units, cost = $24,000 × units, profit = revenue - cost. Note: the demand figures from the casebook are 20,000 cars at $35,000, 30,000 cars at $30,000, and 55,000 cars at $27,500 (likely cumulative demand).
math.answer: Profit-maximizing price is $35,000 (profit = $220M), higher than $30,000 ($180M) or $27,500 ($192.5M).

brainstorming.prompt: What additional pricing or commercial strategies could Green Machine layer on top of the base price to maximize revenue and profits?

categories.name: Price skimming
ideas: Launch at $35,000 to capture premium-WTP customers for first 3 years before competition enters
Reduce price in year 3–4 when Toyota/Honda enter to capture mass market

categories.name: Market segmentation / price discrimination
ideas: Premium trim vs. base trim to serve different WTP segments
Corporate fleet pricing for environmentally conscious companies
Regional pricing if demand concentration varies across Australian states

categories.name: Feature bundling
ideas: Bundle technology/navigation features to raise perceived value and justify higher price
Offer extended warranty bundle to offset customer concern about hybrid maintenance

categories.name: Government incentives
ideas: Highlight the $1,000 subsidy and zero-tax benefit in marketing to lower the effective price for consumers
Lobby for additional incentives as a first-mover before competitors arrive

categories.name: Financing / leasing
ideas: Offer financing that makes monthly payments comparable to a non-hybrid (spreading the premium)
Lease options to lower upfront barrier for cost-sensitive buyers

recommendation: Green Machine should price the hybrid at $35,000 using a price-skimming strategy, which maximizes profit at $220M over the 3-year window before competitors enter

This price is above the value-based ceiling ($25,500–$28,500) but capturable from premium segments (collectors, eco-conscious corporates, status buyers) who place additional non-financial value on the hybrid
risks: If Toyota or Honda accelerate their timeline, Green Machine may face competition sooner than expected, eroding premium pricing power
At $35,000 only 20,000 units are sold in 3 years; Green Machine forgoes the larger volume market
Consumer price sensitivity could be higher than the survey suggests, reducing actual demand at $35,000
next_steps: Conduct deeper segmentation research to identify and size the premium-WTP consumer segment
Develop a phased pricing roadmap: $35,000 for years 1–3, price reduction to ~$27,500–$30,000 when competition arrives
Explore feature-bundle and financing programs to defend margin after the price reduction
